lenses.lens: Funds and accounting, both payment modes (ETH launch mode and legacy ERC-20)
lenses.coverage:
Read in full on disk: src/auction/ERC20EnglishAuction.sol and src/KilimAuction.sol; Kilim.mintMasterpiece; AUDIT.md K-05/K-06/K-09; docs/NATIVE-ETH.md; deploy/mainnet.example.json; test/TestBase.sol, test/NativeRegistration.t.sol (setup), test/mocks/GasBurner.sol; and how site/chain.js sends the native bid. Did not read src/render/*, script/DeployKilim.s.sol or the rest of Kilim.sol (outside this lens).

Dynamic check: I did not add anything to the repo. I built a throwaway Foundry project in the session scratchpad that symlinks src/, node_modules/ and test/ read-only, and ran three local-VM tests there (no network, no broadcast). No out-audit-*/cache-audit-* dirs were created in contracts/; scratch build output was deleted.

Solvency holds; no theft, over-withdrawal or double-claim path found. Checked and found correct:
- Solvency in ETH mode: every bid adds exactly msg.value == amount (_collectBid, L248-250). The previous highestBid is either paid out or moved into refunds[]/refundLiability in the same transaction (L263-271). So balance >= refundLiability + highestBid before settlement and >= refundLiability + proceedsDue after it. Nothing reads address(this).balance, so forced ETH (selfdestruct/coinbase) cannot distort accounting; it is only locked (K-06, accepted).
- One claimant per wei: highestBid becomes proceedsDue once (settle is one-shot via `settled`) and is zeroed before payment (L198-201). An outbid amount is either pushed or deferred, never both, because the self-call's revert is atomic: if the ETH send fails, the whole payOutbidRefund frame reverts, so there is no "sent but also deferred" state.
- Over-withdrawal: withdrawRefund only reads and clears refunds[msg.sender] (L171-175); withdrawProceeds is treasury-only and post-settle; payOutbidRefund/deliverTo/deliverPrize require msg.sender == address(this). An arbitrary `to` only redirects the caller's own entitlement; a reverting `to` rolls everything back.
- Reentrancy: bid, withdrawRefund, withdrawProceeds, settle, claimSymbols, claimPrize, register, registerFor and deliverSymbols share one nonReentrant guard. A refund or prize callback cannot re-enter any of them.
- msg.value: only bid() is payable. There is no receive/fallback, so stray ETH sends revert. A mismatched value reverts with IncorrectPayment; ERC-20 mode rejects any msg.value (L252).
- Self-outbid: the old amount is refunded and the new one collected; net is correct.
- Bounds and rounding: amount <= uint128 max is checked before the multiply in _isNewWinningBid (L226). The predicate's floor division is equivalent to diff >= ceil(highestBid*bps/1e4), which matches minimumBid() (L161-166) once the whole-unit rule (L229) is applied. reservePrice == 0.01 ether is a multiple of the 0.001 ether unit.
- No bid can land between endsAt and settle (L222), so proceedsDue always equals the final highestBid.
- Gas-starving the refund self-call to force a deferral is not feasible: when the inner call runs out of gas, the outer frame keeps at most about 2.4k gas, and the catch block needs at least about 14k (two SSTOREs plus two logs), so the whole bid reverts instead.
- Return-data bombs from the refund recipient are contained by the 150k frame.
- ETH-stuck cases: only forced or donated ETH (K-06), and deferred refunds owed to a contract that can neither receive ETH nor call withdrawRefund (its own limitation). With no bids, the contract holds nothing.

Above info level, this lens found one high-severity issue (bid blocking through the refund callback's variable gas) and one low (prize delivery skippable by a low-gas settle).

lenses.lens: re-entrancy and callbacks (ETH refund call, withdraw recipients, ERC-721 receiver hooks, ERC-1271, self-calls, gas forwarding, returndata, forced reverts)
lenses.coverage:
Read in full, from the working tree: src/auction/ERC20EnglishAuction.sol, src/KilimAuction.sol, src/Kilim.sol, AUDIT.md, plus OpenZeppelin 5.6.1 ReentrancyGuard (storage-based, not transient), ERC721Utils.checkOnERC721Received (bubbles receiver revert data) and SignatureChecker (staticcall, copies only 32 bytes). Checked how site/chain.js sends bid and settle (no explicit gas; only deliverSymbols has a fixed gas limit). I did not review the renderer, deploy script or ERC-20-mode token hooks beyond their callback surface.

No classic re-entrancy (no theft, no double-pay, no double-mint) was found. The two findings above info are both gas-forwarding problems around the self-calls; PoCs were run in an isolated scratch project outside the repo (symlinked src, own out/cache, deleted afterwards). Nothing under the repo was created or modified.

Per external call, state at that moment and what a hostile callee can do:
- bid -> payOutbidRefund -> call{value} to the outbid bidder (ERC20EnglishAuction.sol:265, 300). State is final: new highestBidder/highestBid/endsAt, credits allocated, msg.value collected, guard ENTERED. Every state-changing auction entry point (register, registerFor, bid, withdrawRefund, settle, withdrawProceeds, claimSymbols, deliverSymbols, claimPrize) is nonReentrant and reverts on re-entry. The three unguarded externals (payOutbidRefund, deliverTo, deliverPrize) check only msg.sender == address(this).
- Can a callee make the auction call itself? No. The auction only calls arbitrary addresses with empty calldata (ETH), a staticcall with the isValidSignature selector, or via the collection (where msg.sender is Kilim). It has no receive/fallback and no isValidSignature; `to` == auction or collection is rejected; registerFor(wallet = auction or collection) fails the ERC-1271 check.
- Forced deferral of someone else's refund by under-gassing a bid: not feasible. The catch path's SSTOREs need more than the 1/64 left over. PoC scan of gas limits 60k-400k for receivers costing 0-5 SSTOREs found zero cases of 'bid succeeded and refund deferred'.
- Returndata bombs: `(bool paid,)` and parameterless `catch {}` on all three self-calls do not copy returndata into the outer frame. OZ bubbles receiver revert data through Kilim.mintSymbols/mintMasterpiece, but only inside the gas-capped self-call frame.
- withdrawRefund / withdrawProceeds: balance zeroed before the call, guard held, caller picks `to`; a reverting recipient hurts only the caller.
- claimSymbols / deliverTo -> Kilim.mintSymbols -> onERC721Received: credits, ranges and symbolsClaimed are final first; both guards are held. The recipient can only use unguarded ERC-721 transfer/approve on tokens already received; weave/expand/freeze and any auction entry revert. The AlreadyMinted check per ID blocks double mint.
- settle -> deliverPrize -> Kilim.mintMasterpiece -> onERC721Received(winner): settled/proceedsDue recorded first; a rejecting or gas-burning winner cannot block settle or the treasury's proceeds (PoC: settle with ample gas always succeeds).
- claimPrize: prizeClaimed set first; masterpieceMinted is a second lock.
- Kilim.weave callback: burns, layout and counters final before _safeMint; expand/freeze/weave blocked by Kilim's guard.
- Cross-contract: the guards are separate, but the only Kilim functions reachable from an auction callback are user-owned-token functions, and the only auction functions reachable from a Kilim callback are guarded.
- Read-only re-entrancy: during the refund callback balance exceeds liabilities() by the outgoing refund; during a multi-symbol mint, symbolsMinted/symbolsClaimed already count the whole batch. No contract logic consumes these mid-call. Info only.
- deliverSymbols (ERC-20 mode only) has the correct gasleft pre-check before its self-call; _refundOutbid and _afterSettle do not, which is the root of findings 1 and 2.

lenses.coverage:
Nothing critical or high found in this lens: no path lets one actor permanently block bidding, settlement, refunds, the 1/1 or treasury proceeds for others. One medium, four low, two info.

Read in full on disk (working tree, not HEAD): src/auction/ERC20EnglishAuction.sol, src/KilimAuction.sol, src/Kilim.sol, deploy/mainnet.example.json, deploy/sepolia.example.json, AUDIT.md, docs/NATIVE-ETH.md, test/TestBase.sol, test/GasLimits.t.sol, test/mocks/GasBurner.sol, the head of test/NativeRegistration.t.sol. Not reviewed: src/render/*, registration-relayer/server.mjs.

Proof tests ran in a throwaway Foundry project in the session scratchpad that imported the on-disk sources; it is deleted. Nothing in the repo was modified and no out-audit/cache-audit dirs were created.

Measured:
- One transaction registers 100 wallets and places the opening bid: 6,839,759 gas.
- Bid that outbids an EOA: 115,634 gas. Bid that outbids a contract burning the whole 150k refund allowance: 256,782 gas, refund deferred correctly.
- Under-gassing a bid to force an honest wallet's refund into the pull path: swept gas limits 60k-600k against receivers needing 5k, 30k, 80k and 140k; no gas limit succeeds with a deferral. The bid reverts whole instead.
- Under-gassing settle(): cannot fail delivery to an EOA winner or a contract whose receiver hook costs up to 25k; can at 50k and above (finding 3).
- claimSymbols(64) from one range: 1,890,295 gas.

Checked and found correct:
- registrationCount cannot exceed 100: `>=` guard at ERC20EnglishAuction.sol:150, single increment, nonReentrant. The `!=` gate at :217 is therefore equivalent to `<`.
- The treasury can neither register nor bid.
- registerFor replay is blocked by registered[wallet]; the domain binds chain and contract; a front-run signature only registers the wallet that signed.
- A top bidder that rejects ETH or burns gas cannot block the next bid: try/catch at :265 with a 150k cap, no returndata copy. Extra cost is bounded at about 141k gas, far below the 16,777,216 per-transaction cap.
- withdrawRefund(to) and withdrawProceeds(to) take an alternative recipient and roll back on failure. ETH balance always covers highestBid plus refundLiability.
- Unbounded extension is self-limiting: each extension needs a bid at least 10% higher that stays escrowed and becomes the winning obligation. Six extensions an hour multiply the price by 1.77; a full day of 10-minute extensions by about 9e5.
- settle() cannot be made to revert by the winner: _afterSettle is a caught self-call. claimPrize(to) remains available after a failed delivery, and a successful delivery cannot be followed by a second mint.
- claimSymbols loops are bounded by quantity <= 64 (at most 64 chunks); the checklist's worst case of 6.75M is under the cap. Kilim.mintSymbols is limited to 64 per call. Weave and expand at 256 cells are 9.77M and 9.47M per the repo's gas tests.
- deliverSymbols has a 256-entry scan bound, a 64-symbol batch and a 63/64 gas guard at KilimAuction.sol:190, and is disabled in ETH mode (:179).
- With no bids, or fewer than 100 registrations, no ETH is ever held, so nothing can be stuck.

lenses.lens: registration and signatures (register, registerFor, registrationDigest, _register, EIP712 base)
lenses.coverage:
Read in full on disk (working tree, not HEAD): contracts/src/auction/ERC20EnglishAuction.sol, contracts/src/KilimAuction.sol; test/SponsoredRegistration.t.sol; docs/NATIVE-ETH.md; the registration parts of AUDIT.md, README.md, checklists/1-pre-deploy.md, deploy/mainnet.example.json, site/auction.part.html, site/src-auction.html (typed data and register flow); registration-relayer/README.md and the gas/simulation lines of server.mjs; OpenZeppelin 5.6.1 SignatureChecker, ECDSA and EIP712 as pinned in node_modules. I did not run forge and wrote no files (my task did not permit adding PoCs), so gas figures below are estimates, not measurements.

Nothing in this lens reaches critical or high: registration never moves, escrows or authorises ETH or NFTs, and the `registered` flag is read by nothing except _register itself. The findings are about what the 100-wallet gate does not guarantee.

Checked and found correct:
- Domain binding: EIP712("Kilim Registration","1") (ERC20EnglishAuction.sol:94); OZ _domainSeparatorV4 rebuilds the separator when block.chainid or address(this) differs from the cached values, so a signature cannot be replayed across chains, after a fork, or on another deployment. test/SponsoredRegistration.t.sol covers chain and second-auction replay.
- Typehash: "Register(address wallet,uint256 deadline)" (line 81) matches abi.encode(REGISTER_TYPEHASH, wallet, deadline) (line 144) and the site's typed data (site/src-auction.html:2462-2469), including the EIP712Domain field order.
- Replay: registered[wallet] is a one-shot guard shared by register() and registerFor() (line 155); no nonce is needed because the only effect is idempotent.
- Malleability: OZ ECDSA rejects high-s and a zero recovered signer, and accepts only 65-byte signatures; a malleated signature could not double-register anyway.
- wallet == address(0): rejected explicitly (line 135) and by OZ (recovered zero returns an error).
- Treasury: rejected in _register (line 154) on both paths.
- Deadline: block.timestamp > deadline reverts (line 133); the signature is valid in the deadline block itself. No upper bound on deadline, which is harmless because the signature authorises only a one-shot registration for this auction.
- ERC-1271: verification is a staticcall, so a hostile isValidSignature cannot re-enter or change state; OZ copies only 32 bytes of returndata (no returndata bomb); a wallet that changes its answer only affects whether it is registered at that moment. registerFor and register are nonReentrant.
- Gate comparison: _handleBid uses registrationCount != REGISTRATION_TARGET (line 217) while _register refuses at >= REGISTRATION_TARGET (line 150) and increments by exactly one (line 158), so the count can never exceed 100 and != is equivalent to <. Registration cannot overshoot.
- Cannot be permanently stuck below 100: anyone can add wallets at gas cost, and no funds are held before unlock. Registration is refused before startsAt and in ERC-20 mode (line 149).
- Unregistered wallets can bid once the count is 100: _handleBid checks only the count, never registered[msg.sender]. This is intended and stated in docs/NATIVE-ETH.md:9 and site/auction.part.html:223 ("Anyone can then place the opening bid").
- Registering a contract that cannot receive ETH or NFTs has no consequence: registration grants nothing; refund and prize paths have their own fallbacks.

lenses.lens: symbols, credits and the collection (KilimAuction rewards/claims/delivery, Kilim.sol mint/weave/expand/freeze/owner/royalty)
lenses.coverage:
Nothing above LOW in this lens. I found no way to mint for free beyond the owner-accepted K-01, mint twice, burn someone else's token, or brick a token.

Read in full, on disk (working tree, not HEAD): src/KilimAuction.sol, src/auction/ERC20EnglishAuction.sol, src/Kilim.sol, src/render/IKilimRenderer.sol, the token-metadata and layout-validation parts of src/render/KilimRenderer.sol (lines 90-125, 340-580), deploy/*.json, the launch constants and refusals in script/DeployKilim.s.sol, AUDIT.md, README.md, docs/NATIVE-ETH.md, test/NativeRegistration.t.sol, test/TestBase.sol, test/mocks/Receiver.sol. I did not read KilimWriter.sol or the renderer's drawing assembly (another lens).

Dynamic checks ran in a throwaway Foundry project in the session scratchpad, symlinked to src/ and node_modules/, local VM only. Nothing was added or changed in the repo; the scratch project is deleted.

Checked and found correct:
- **Reward maths.** rewardForBid = min(amount / tokenUnit, maxSymbolsPerBid, symbolCap - symbolsAllocated) cannot underflow, because symbolsAllocated only grows by a reward already bounded by the remainder. In ETH mode tokenUnit is SYMBOL_PRICE and bids are whole multiples, so 0.01 ETH earns exactly 10.
- **ID reservation.** firstSymbolId = 2 + symbolsAllocated gives disjoint, gapless ranges inside 2..symbolCap+1. The uint128 casts are safe (symbolCap <= uint32 max - 2, enforced by Kilim's constructor).
- **expectedFirstSymbolId / minimumReward.** Zero reward with a nonzero expected ID reverts; a partial reward at the cap is caught by minimumReward. A failed ETH bid reverts whole, so credits and the queue push roll back.
- **Claims.** In _claim the unclaimed ranges from the cursor always sum to symbolCredits, so ranges[cursor] cannot go out of bounds. Credits, cursor and range state are final before any mint callback. A reverting receiver reverts the whole claim, so no credits are lost.
- **No double mint.** Every state-changing auction entry is nonReentrant; deliverTo, deliverPrize and payOutbidRefund require msg.sender == address(this). Kilim.mintSymbols also refuses any ID whose kindOf is not None, so a burned ID (consumedBy != 0) can never be minted again.
- **ETH-mode delivery revert is complete.** deliverSymbols reverts at KilimAuction.sol:179, and deliverTo is reachable only from deliverSymbols. No interleaving of claim and delivery exists in ETH mode.
- **ERC-20 delivery (legacy).** A failed deliverTo rolls back its own _claim. The gasleft check (allowance + allowance/63 + 50k) guarantees the inner call its full allowance, so a low gas limit cannot skip a wallet. A manual claim before delivery leaves take == 0 and the cursor advances.
- **Mint authorisation.** mintSymbols and mintMasterpiece are onlyMinter; minter is the immutable auction, created in its constructor. The masterpiece is guarded twice (prizeClaimed and masterpieceMinted). Symbol, artwork and 1/1 ID ranges are disjoint.
- **Weave / expand / freeze.** _consumeLayout requires kindOf == Symbol, ownerOf == msg.sender (approved operators cannot burn), rejects duplicates through lastRevision == revision, rejects symbols consumed by another artwork, and requires retained == oldLength, so every earlier source is kept exactly once. An invalid appearance reverts atomically after the burns. Cells fit 32 bits; pack and unpack match. expand requires the artwork owner, not frozen, a matching revision and strictly more cells. Frozen artworks still transfer.
- **Renderer bounds match.** Kilim's layout limits (columns, rows >= 2, at most 256 cells, three appearances) equal KilimRenderer._artworkBound, so a layout Kilim accepts is not rejected by the renderer's layout check.
- **Transfers.** _update blocks transfers to the collection and the auction. Burns pass through.
- **Owner role.** It can only transfer or renounce itself, set the royalty receiver and set the collection text and link. It has no path to tokens, art, minting or funds.
- **contractURI.** _escapeJson escapes the quote, the backslash and all control characters below 0x20 as \u00XX; the hex digits are correct.
- **Interfaces.** supportsInterface returns true for ERC-721, ERC-165, ERC-2981 (0x2a55205a) and ERC-4906 (0x49064906).

Measured:
- One contract laddering self-outbids in a single transaction (62 bids, 5.2M gas) reached a 4.886 ETH top bid holding 53,367 symbol credits, with every earlier bid refunded.
- settle() with about 148k gas records settlement but drops the 1/1 delivery when the winner's receiver hook makes two or more fresh storage writes. It could not be forced for an EOA winner or a hook with zero or one write.

Not read: the renderer, weave/expand, the rest of the deploy script (outside this lens).

Launch numbers used: reserve 0.01 ETH, increment 1000 bps, unit 0.001 ETH, duration 86400, extension 600, symbolCap = maxSymbolsPerBid = 1,000,000.

I ran four attack models on a local Foundry VM. The PoC lived in a shadow project in the session scratchpad that symlinked src/ and node_modules; nothing was added to the repo, nothing was broadcast, and no out-audit/cache-audit dirs were created in contracts/. All five tests passed:
- One-contract self-outbid ladder to pool exhaustion: 93 bids, top bid 93.862 ETH, 1,000,000 credits, about 7.2M gas.
- Ladder to 5 ETH: 62 bids, 53,367 credits, full refund when outbid.
- 100 sybil registrations in one transaction: about 8.06M gas, 0.01 ETH recycled.
- Leader with a switchable receive(): competing bid costs 117,784 gas in cheap mode and 300,552 in burn mode; a bid sent with 1.5x or 2x the cheap estimate reverts.
- settle() gas sweep from 40k to 400k: no gas value makes settle succeed with the prize undelivered for an EOA winner; minimum for settle with delivery is about 114k.

Checked and found correct:
- **Bid ladder.** minimumBid() and the retained thirdweb predicate agree: ceil 10%, then rounded up to 0.001 ETH.
- **uint128 bound.** Amounts above uint128 are rejected, and in ETH mode msg.value == amount, so no overflow or lock-out bid is possible.
- **Close boundary.** bid is refused at timestamp >= endsAt and settle is allowed at >= endsAt, so they never overlap. A late bid never shortens the close.
- **Timestamps.** Post-merge slot timestamps give a proposer no useful control. Censoring competitors through the 10-minute window needs about 50 consecutive cooperating proposers.
- **Forced refund deferral.** A third party cannot force the leader's refund into the pull path by starving gas. If the inner call gets less than 150k, the outer frame keeps under 2.4k, cannot pay for the catch-path SSTOREs, and the whole bid reverts.
- **Deferred refunds.** They are always withdrawable via withdrawRefund(to); a failed withdrawal rolls back.
- **Hostile winner.** A winner who makes deliverPrize fail gains nothing: settled and proceedsDue are recorded first, prizeClaimed rolls back with the self-call, and claimPrize(to) remains.
- **Return data.** No return-bomb: return data is not copied in _pay or in the try/catch.
- **Re-entry.** A refund or prize callback cannot re-enter; every entry point is nonReentrant.
- **Forced ETH.** It does not affect accounting.
- **Seller.** The treasury cannot bid or register.
- **Blocking a bid cheaply.** A competitor's bid can only be made to revert by placing a higher or range-moving bid, which costs the attacker a 10% raise and the lead. Apart from the gas mechanism in finding 1, there is no cheap way to win the 1/1 below a competing bid.

Nothing I found lets anyone steal ETH or NFTs. The worst an honest bidder loses is gas, expected symbols, or (finding 1) the chance to land a bid.

Nothing above low severity found in this lens. Everything was checked by reading the on-disk working tree; I ran no forge tests and wrote no PoC (this task did not permit adding files), so the gas figures in finding 1 are reasoned estimates, not measurements.

Read in full: script/DeployKilim.s.sol, src/KilimAuction.sol, src/auction/ERC20EnglishAuction.sol, src/Kilim.sol, src/render/IKilimRenderer.sol, deploy/*.json, site/chains/*.json, scripts/site-config.mjs, AUDIT.md, docs/NATIVE-ETH.md, checklists/1-pre-deploy.md, launch/DECISIONS.md. Checked and found correct:
- **Chain-1 pins match the ETH design.** paymentToken zero, tokenDecimals 18, reservePrice 0.01 ether (the constructor also forces it to equal REGISTRATION_BALANCE in ETH mode), incrementBps 1000, duration 86400, extensionWindow 600, symbolCap and maxSymbolsPerBid 1,000,000, maxCells 256, treasury and collectionOwner 0xd6647Eeec0c8D810C546f2ab8e025D4664d833Ac. deploy/mainnet.example.json and sepolia.example.json carry the same values. On chain 1 the script refuses run(), a skipped nonce check and a zero minLeadSeconds.
- **Constructor validation.** The ETH unit is SYMBOL_PRICE regardless of decimals; maxSymbolsPerBid must be at most symbolCap; symbolCap is bounded by uint64 in the auction and uint32-2 in Kilim; treasury cannot be zero, the auction or the collection; startsAt must be in the future; extensionWindow must be at most duration.
- **Address and nonce assumptions.** The auction address is predicted from the deployer nonce and re-checked; Kilim is created by the auction and read back in _checkAuction. The uint16 cast of motifCount cannot truncate silently because the untruncated value is compared with the renderer's.
- **Renderer and store integrity.** Chunk addresses, sizes, hashes and section hashes are recomputed from the bytes to be deployed; foreign code at a chunk address is refused. The renderer address comes from CREATE2 over the initcode, so front-running the store deployment only produces the same contracts. The renderer's immutables (the three hashes, section offsets, still motifs, TABLES) are in its runtime code, so rendererHash commits to content even though the chunk list is in storage.
- **Renderer failure cannot block anything that moves value.** Kilim calls the renderer only in its constructor and in tokenURI (a staticcall). Mints, transfers, weave, expand, settle, claimSymbols and claimPrize never touch it. Renderer layout bounds match Kilim's (2 to 256 cells, same three appearances).
- **tokenURI read gas** (1/1 about 22.4M, heaviest artwork about 30.4M with the 812 pack) is already documented as K-03.
- **Site against the contract ABI.** contracts/abi/KilimAuction.json matches the on-disk source (the sourceSha256 entries in audit/build-manifest.json match every src file). Every signature in site/abi.js exists with the same types. In ETH mode the site sends bid(amount, minimumReward, 0) with value equal to amount, register() with no value, and claim/withdraw/settle calls with no value. The EIP-712 domain ("Kilim Registration", "1", chainId, auction) and the Register(address wallet,uint256 deadline) type match the contract. The site checks paymentToken is zero and tokenUnit is 1e15 at startup, and deliverSymbols is hidden in ETH mode. I found no call that would revert or send the wrong value for real users.
- **Automatic refund cannot be gas-starved.** The catch path needs two storage writes (about 45k gas), so whenever it can complete, the refund call received its full 150k.

lenses.lens: Test adequacy by mutation (working tree, ETH launch mode)
lenses.coverage:
Nothing above medium found. No mutant exposed a theft or stuck-funds bug in the on-disk code; what the run found is missing tests, plus one low-severity behaviour in settle().

METHOD
- Read src/KilimAuction.sol and src/auction/ERC20EnglishAuction.sol in full, `git diff -- src/`, test/NativeRegistration.t.sol, test/SponsoredRegistration.t.sol, test/TestBase.sol, test/AuctionInvariants.t.sol, and the mint functions in src/Kilim.sol. For the other test files, script/DeployKilim.s.sol and AUDIT.md I read only the test-name lists, the reserve/payment-token checks and the K-01..K-09 headings.
- Deviation from the task text: I did not create test/poc/mutants/ in the repo. I copied src/, test/, script/, deploy/ to a private scratchpad directory, applied each mutant to the copied src/ and ran the real, unmodified suite against it. This is true mutation testing rather than renamed copies, and it cannot break another agent's forge build. The repo was never written to; the scratch copy is deleted; no out-audit-*/cache-audit-* dirs exist.
- Baseline in the copy: 232/232 tests pass. Mutants ran against 118 tests in 10 suites (everything except test/render/*, CompositionInvariants and Kilim.t.sol, which do not touch the auction).
- 93 mutants run one at a time: 77 single-point mutants of the changed code and its guards, and 16 mode-conditional ("ETH only") mutants to see which shared behaviours are tested only through ERC-20 fixtures. 60 killed, 32 survived (reported below), 1 failed to compile (bid not payable).

KILLED (the existing suite does protect these)
- Payment: msg.value != amount flipped to < or >, or dropped; msg.value != 0 dropped in ERC-20 mode; added receive().
- Registration: bid gate removed; cap >= changed to >; AlreadyRegistered dropped; balance check dropped or <=; registered flag not set; counter not incremented; target 99 or 101; tx.origin instead of msg.sender.
- registerFor: deadline check dropped; signature check dropped; registers msg.sender; digest without deadline; digest without domain separator; ERC-1271 path disabled.
- Refunds: failed ETH transfer ignored; payOutbidRefund self-guard dropped; REFUND_GAS 2,300 and 20,000; try/catch removed; refundLiability += dropped; refunds = instead of +=; never push; self-outbid refund skipped.
- withdrawRefund: nonReentrant dropped; refunds = 0 dropped; liability decrement dropped; pays msg.sender instead of `to`.

findings.title: Current top bidder can make rivals' ETH bids run out of gas by switching its refund receiver between cheap and gas-burning (no gas floor before the refund self-call)
findings.location: src/auction/ERC20EnglishAuction.sol:26 (REFUND_GAS), :263-272 (_refundOutbid), :276-279 (payOutbidRefund), :298-302 (_pay); src/KilimAuction.sol:146-147; compare the guard at src/KilimAuction.sol:190; site/chain.js:875-878 (native bid sent with no gas limit)
findings.description:
In ETH mode every bid that outbids someone runs the previous leader's code. _refundOutbid does `try this.payOutbidRefund{gas: REFUND_GAS}` (150,000) and _pay forwards all of it to the outbid address via call{value}. `{gas:}` is only a cap: if less is left, the EVM forwards 63/64 of what remains. There is no gasleft() check before the try (deliverSymbols has one at KilimAuction.sol:190; this path does not).

The gas a bid needs therefore depends on code the current leader controls, and it can differ between the wallet's eth_estimateGas and actual execution. If the receiver burns everything it is given, the bid keeps only 1/64 of its remaining gas, which is less than the catch path needs (two fresh SSTOREs for refunds[] and refundLiability, about 45k), so the whole bid reverts out of gas instead of deferring the refund.

Reviewer measurements on the on-disk code in a local VM (execution gas; reviewers differ slightly depending on whether the receiver reverts into the deferred path):
- Bid over a contract with a cheap receive(): about 116k-118k.
- Same bid when receive() burns its allowance: about 256k (burn then accept) to about 300k (burn then defer).
- A bid sent with 1.5x the cheap estimate reverted, and one reviewer saw it still revert at 2x; highestBidder remained the attacker. It succeeded only from about 2.2x, or about 293k-320k absolute.
- A receiver that burns only when `block.basefee != 0` passed a zero-basefee simulation and failed on-chain at 1.5x. A variant keyed on tx.gasprice == 0 was suggested but not tested.

The site sends the native bid with no explicit gas (site/chain.js:878; txOf only sets gas when c.gas is given), so the wallet's estimate with its usual buffer is what gets signed.

Nothing is taken from the contract. The impact is cheap manipulation of the auction outcome plus lost gas for honest bidders. A blocked bid does not extend the close, so in the final window the leader can win below the real market price. The 150k cap bounds the extra gas but does not remove the estimate-versus-execution gap. Existing tests cover a reverting and a re-entering ETH recipient, not one that burns gas. Reviewers state this is not covered by K-09, which considers the refund failing for the recipient, not the gas-estimate gap for the next bidder.

Severity argued: high (two reviewers), medium (one).
findings.exploit_scenario:
1. Mallory deploys a bidder contract whose receive() is cheap by default and burns all forwarded gas when armed. She can arm it with a ~28-30k gas transaction, or key it on block.prevrandao, a blockhash coin flip or block.basefee != 0 so it differs between simulation and inclusion with no transaction at all. An EIP-7702-delegated EOA works the same way.
2. In the last extension window she bids through it and becomes highestBidder (for example at 2 ETH).
3. Alice bids 2.2 ETH from the site. Her wallet simulates the cheap path (about 118k execution, about 140k total) and signs with a 1.5x limit (about 177k-205k).
4. Mallory sees Alice's pending transaction and front-runs it by arming the receiver (or relies on the stateless trick).
5. In Alice's transaction the refund self-call gets 63/64 of what is left, the receiver burns it, the catch path's SSTORE runs out of gas and the bid reverts. Alice pays the gas; Mallory is still leader and endsAt is not extended.
6. Mallory disarms so the next estimate is cheap again, and repeats for every competing bid until endsAt, then settles and takes the 1/1 at her low bid. Cost: two small transactions per blocked bid. Only bidders who set a manual gas limit of about 320k-350k or use a private mempool get through, and they also pay the extra gas Mallory burns. Collectors lose gas and the piece; the artist receives less than the market price.
findings.recommendation:
Fix in the contract before deployment, since it is immutable afterwards. In _refundOutbid, before the try, revert unless gasleft() covers the full allowance plus the 1/64 held back plus the catch path and BidPlaced event, for example `if (gasleft() < REFUND_GAS + REFUND_GAS / 63 + 60_000) revert`. This is the pattern deliverSymbols already uses. With that floor, any gas estimate in any leader mode includes the worst case, so toggling the callback can no longer make a correctly estimated bid fail.

Also lower REFUND_GAS in ETH mode: an EOA needs none and a Safe needs under 10k, so 30-50k is enough and shrinks the gas a hostile leader can charge every later bidder.

Defence in depth: have the site send native bids with an explicit gas limit (estimate + at least 250k, or a fixed 350k-400k; unused gas is refunded), as it already does for deliverSymbols.

Add a test with a mode-switching receiver that asserts a bid sent with the cheap-mode estimate still succeeds (or reverts cleanly at estimate time).

re-entrancy and callbacks (ETH refund call, withdraw recipients, ERC-721 receiver hooks, ERC-1271, self-calls, gas forwarding, returndata, forced reverts)
economics, timing and MEV

findings.title: settle() has no gas floor before the prize self-call: a low-gas call skips delivery of the 1/1 to a contract winner, and the 1/1 is lost if that contract cannot call claimPrize
findings.location: src/KilimAuction.sol:259-264 (_afterSettle), :62 (PRIZE_GAS), :267-273 (deliverPrize), :277-286 (claimPrize); compare the guard at :189-190; src/auction/ERC20EnglishAuction.sol:181-189 (settle); site/chain.js:1346 (settle sent with no gas limit)
findings.description:
_afterSettle does `try this.deliverPrize{gas: PRIZE_GAS}() {} catch { emit PrizeDeliveryFailed }` with no check that 500k (plus the 1/64 kept back) is actually available. Under EIP-150 the self-call receives at most 63/64 of the remaining gas. The catch path needs only one event and the reentrancy-guard reset (a few thousand gas), so if the mint runs out of gas settle() still succeeds with `settled = true` and prizeClaimed == false. It cannot be retried: settle() then reverts AlreadySettled and deliverPrize is self-only. The only remaining path is claimPrize, which requires msg.sender == highestBidder. deliverSymbols has exactly this protection (`if (gasleft() < allowance + allowance / 63 + 50_000) break;`); settlement does not.

settle() is permissionless, so the caller chooses how much gas the delivery gets.

Reviewer measurements on the on-disk code (settle gas limits that succeed without delivering the prize):
- EOA winner, or a receiver hook costing up to about 25k gas / zero or one storage write per two reviewers: not forceable; the mint (about 100k-114k) is too cheap for the retained 1/64 to cover the catch, so settle reverts instead. One reviewer did get a hit with a single-SSTORE hook at 148k-161k.
- Hook with two or more fresh storage writes, or costing 50k, 100k, 200k or 400k: settle() at about 147,710-148,000 gas succeeds with the 1/1 not minted.
- Five SSTOREs: 148k-253k. Fifteen SSTOREs: 148k-489k. A hook using about 230k: 148k-352k (a full-gas settle uses 340,241 and delivers).
- One reviewer estimated the affected range from reading the code only (hooks above about 120k); the measured results above show it starts lower.

So any winner with non-trivial receiver code, well inside the documented 500k allowance, can be denied automatic delivery by a third party. No funds are lost and proceedsDue is recorded correctly. For a smart wallet that can make arbitrary calls this is a nuisance (it calls claimPrize(to)). For a winner contract that relies on the documented delivery and has no way to call claimPrize (a bidding pool, vault or simple bidder contract), the 1/1 can never be minted, while the treasury still withdraws the full winning bid.

This can also happen without malice: eth_estimateGas looks for the lowest limit at which settle succeeds, which is the limit where delivery fails, and the site sends settle with no gas field. There is no test for this path; the nearest is Delivery.t.sol:108 for deliverSymbols.

Severity argued: medium (one reviewer), low (five reviewers).
findings.exploit_scenario:
1. A collector group wins through a pool contract that implements onERC721Received (records the token, about 60k gas) and a bid function, but no claimPrize call, because settlement is documented to send the 1/1 to the winner.
2. After endsAt a losing bidder or griefer calls `settle{gas: 150_000}()`.
3. deliverPrize receives about 63/64 of what is left, the mint runs out of gas inside Kilim.mintMasterpiece or the receiver hook, the catch emits PrizeDeliveryFailed, and settle succeeds.
4. The auction is settled for good, proceedsDue goes to the treasury, and the only way to mint token 1 is claimPrize from the pool contract, which it cannot call. The winners paid in full and the 1/1 never exists. Attacker cost: one transaction of about 148k gas.

Reverting is safe because settle() is permissionless and can be retried; gas estimation then returns a sufficient limit.

Optionally add a permissionless retry (for example a function that, after settlement and while !prizeClaimed, safe-mints to highestBidder only, never to an arbitrary recipient) so delivery never depends on the winner being able to call claimPrize.

findings.title: One transaction can fill all 100 registration slots with recycled 0.01 ETH and place the opening bid, so one actor chooses when the 24-hour clock starts and locks real supporters out
findings.location: src/auction/ERC20EnglishAuction.sol:106 (reserve forced to 0.01 ETH), :125-127 (register), :147-159 (_register, balance check at :156, cap at :150), :217-219 (gate on count only), :235-238 (clock starts at first bid); src/KilimAuction.sol:135; deploy/mainnet.example.json (duration 86400, reservePrice 0.01 ETH); docs/NATIVE-ETH.md:23; site/auction.part.html:224
findings.description:
_register only checks `wallet.balance >= 0.01 ether` at call time (line 156) and that the address is not yet registered (line 155). It takes no deposit, has no code-size or tx.origin check, and nothing limits registrations per transaction or ties a registration to a person. The same 0.01 ETH can be passed through 100 throwaway contracts that each call register() from their constructor and return the ETH. The 100th registration unlocks bidding (line 217 checks only the count, not who registered), and the first bid starts the clock (lines 235-238), so the same transaction can also place the 0.01 ETH opening bid.

Measured by two reviewers in scratch tests: 6,839,759 gas including the opening bid, and about 8.06M gas for the registrations alone; a third estimated about 8M. All are under the 16,777,216 per-transaction cap. Capital needed is 0.02 ETH, of which 0.01 is the bid itself. Afterwards registrationCount was 100, endsAt was now + 24h, an honest wallet's register() reverted with RegistrationClosed, and with no competing bid settle() delivered token 1 to the attacker.

Consequences:
- The 100-wallet gate gives no protection and no pacing.
- Registration closes for good at 100 (line 150), so real supporters can be shut out of all slots and pay gas for reverted transactions. The site shows "Register interest (n/100)", so the count is a public moment.
- The attacker, not the artist or community, decides when the only 24-hour window runs: as early as the first block at startsAt. Because the constructor forces reservePrice == 0.01 ETH in native mode (line 106), the 1/1 can be opened at 0.01 ETH at startsAt itself.
- If the window is not noticed in time, the 1/1 goes at the 0.01 ETH reserve.
- The opening bidder deterministically takes the first symbol IDs (KilimAuction.sol:135), whose traits are fixed by ID.
- The seller can do the same, so "100 wallets registered" is not evidence of 100 interested people.
- Sponsored registration (registerFor) pays gas for whichever wallets ask, so a sybil can also spend the sponsor's budget.

The docs and site already say registration counts wallets, not people, and that funds can move (docs/NATIVE-ETH.md:23, site/auction.part.html:224). They do not cover the atomic one-transaction fill, the lock-out of real registrants, or the attacker choosing the clock start. No bidder funds are at risk; the exposure is the sale outcome and supporters' expectations.

Severity argued: medium (two reviewers), low (one).
findings.exploit_scenario:
1. Before startsAt the attacker deploys a helper/factory contract.
2. In the first block with timestamp >= startsAt (say 03:00 in the artist's timezone) they call helper.run{value: 0.02 ether}(auction).
3. The helper loops 100 times: `new Child{value: 0.01 ether}(auction)`, whose constructor calls auction.register() (msg.sender is the child, balance is 0.01 ETH, check passes) and sends the ETH back to the helper.
4. The helper then calls auction.bid{value: 0.01 ether}(0.01 ether, 10, 0). endsAt = now + 86400.
5. Cost: about 6.84M-8M gas (roughly 0.007 ETH at 1 gwei, 0.016 ETH at 2 gwei) plus the refundable 0.01 ETH bid.
6. Every supporter who planned to register gets RegistrationClosed and pays for a reverted transaction. The auction ends 24 hours later whether or not the launch was announced for that moment. If nobody outbids in time (plus extensions) the attacker settles and takes the 1/1 for 0.01 ETH and the artist receives 0.01 ETH; if someone does, the attacker gets the 0.01 ETH back automatically and keeps the first 10 symbol IDs. The attacker can optionally follow with the self-outbid ladder of F-04.
findings.recommendation:
Decide what registration is for and make the contract match before it is frozen:
- If it is only a social counter or ceremony, say publicly that it gives no protection, that registering gives no bidding right, that the slots may fill instantly, and that one party can complete all 100 registrations and place the opening bid in one transaction the instant startsAt passes. Treat startsAt as the real opening time and have the artist and collectors ready then. At minimum add that sentence to the site terms and NATIVE-ETH.md.
- To stop an attacker choosing the clock, add a separate immutable bidding-open time (registration opens at startsAt, bids only after a later biddingOpensAt), or a fixed delay between the 100th registration and the first accepted bid.
- To make the 100 slots harder to sybil, require a per-wallet refundable 0.01 ETH deposit held until bidding opens, so 100 registrations lock 1 ETH. A `msg.sender == tx.origin` or `code.length == 0` check alone only forces 100 separate transactions.
- If the 100 are meant to be real supporters, use an allow-list (a Merkle root, or a signer the artist controls) instead of a balance check.
- Alternatively remove the gate and rely on startsAt alone, since it adds a failure mode without adding protection.
- If the artist wants a floor on the sale price, allow a reserve above 0.01 ETH instead of hard-wiring it at line 106.
- Keep the sponsor relayer behind its own per-wallet checks so a sybil cannot drain its budget.

findings.title: Self-outbidding with automatically refunded ETH lets one actor take the whole 1,000,000-symbol pool in one transaction at a top bid of about 91-94 ETH (K-01 in ETH mode; the inherited cap is now binding)
findings.location: src/KilimAuction.sol:130-149 (_bid), :152-154 (rewardForBid); src/auction/ERC20EnglishAuction.sol:215-244, :263-272 (_refundOutbid); script/DeployKilim.s.sol:79-80 and :425-428; deploy/mainnet.example.json:25-26 (symbolCap 1000000, maxSymbolsPerBid 1000000); AUDIT.md K-01; launch/DECISIONS.md
findings.description:
This is the mechanism the owner accepted as K-01, restated because the on-disk ETH configuration changes the numbers the acceptance was based on.

rewardForBid pays amount / 0.001 ETH credits per bid, capped only by maxSymbolsPerBid (set equal to symbolCap, so no per-bid cap) and by symbolCap - symbolsAllocated. Nothing stops msg.sender from outbidding itself, the outbid amount is refunded automatically inside the same call, and credits are never removed. A single contract can therefore climb the minimum 10% ladder against itself in one transaction, recycling the same ETH; only the last bid stays escrowed.

Measured on a local VM by two reviewers:
- 62 bids in one transaction, about 4.9M-5.2M gas, ended with a 4.886 ETH top bid and 53,367 symbol credits (an honest single 4.886 ETH bid earns 4,886). All 48.48 ETH of earlier bids came back. That is about 10,900 credits per ETH of final top bid.
- 93 bids from 0.01 ETH to 93.862 ETH allocate all 1,000,000 symbols to one address for about 7.2M gas, under the 16.7M per-transaction cap. Other reviewers extrapolated the threshold as about 91-92 ETH. Peak balance is about 180 ETH for an instant (the previous bid is refunded only after the next is paid); the difference can be flash-borrowed.

After that rewardForBid returns 0 for everyone: later supporters' bids still succeed but earn no symbols, and minimumReward is their only protection.

Outcomes for the attacker:
- If anyone bids 103.249 ETH or more, the attacker gets all 93.862 ETH back and keeps every symbol for gas.
- If nobody does, they own the 1/1 and the whole symbol supply for 93.862 ETH.
- If the attacker is the seller's own second wallet (K-07), the ETH returns through withdrawProceeds, so the cost is gas either way.
- The ladderer also takes the lowest and rarest IDs first, since traits are public (K-02).

AUDIT.md K-01 says that with the launch settings there is no binding cap and farming "cannot exhaust a pool" / "inflates supply instead". That was written for USDC (which bound at about $91k); with the on-disk ETH config the chain-1 guard pins symbolCap = maxSymbolsPerBid = 1,000,000, the pool is exhausted after 1,000 ETH of cumulative accepted bids, and one actor can reach it in the first block bidding opens (see F-03). launch/DECISIONS.md itself lists "revalidation of inherited total/per-bid allocation limits" as unresolved and says not to carry forward the old pool-exhaustion numbers; the script carries them forward.

No honest bidder loses ETH; they lose the symbols they were told bids earn.

Severity argued: medium (economics reviewer), low (deployment reviewer), info (symbols reviewer, as a restatement of accepted K-01).
findings.exploit_scenario:
1. At startsAt the attacker's factory registers 100 throwaway wallets in one transaction, unlocking bidding (F-03).
2. In the next transaction, attacker contract C, holding 94 ETH plus a flash loan of about 86 ETH, loops `auction.bid{value: m}(m, 0, 0)` with m = minimumBid() 93 times. Each bid refunds C's previous bid automatically.
3. End state: symbolsAllocated = 1,000,000, symbolCredits[C] = 1,000,000 starting at symbol ID 2, C leads at 93.862 ETH, flash loan repaid.
4. Every supporter who bids afterwards gets a reward of 0. The site quotes 0, or the bid reverts with RewardSlippage if the quote was taken earlier.
5. If a collector outbids C at 103.249 ETH, C receives 93.862 ETH back in that transaction and later mints all 1,000,000 symbols with claimSymbols, for gas only. With smaller capital P the attacker takes about 10,900 x P credits, diluting supporters and taking the best IDs.
findings.recommendation:
Have the owner re-confirm K-01 against the ETH numbers before the pins are treated as final, and record the decision in DECISIONS.md. Options, in order of how much they change the accepted economics:
- Set maxSymbolsPerBid well below symbolCap (for example the reward of a few ETH), so one bid cannot take a large share, the ladder is much longer and more expensive in gas, and a single late bid cannot take the remainder.
- Reward only the increment over the bidder's own previous bid, or skip the reward when the outbid address == msg.sender. This removes the single-wallet loop; two colluding wallets can still alternate.
- Size symbolCap so it cannot bind at any plausible price, or state on the site that the pool can run out, that symbols can be collected with refunded ETH, and that one bidder can take the pool.

At minimum correct the AUDIT.md K-01 text ("cannot exhaust a pool") to the ETH numbers and the roughly 91-94 ETH threshold, and the site copy. Keep minimumReward set to the quoted reward, as chain.js already does, so supporters are never silently given fewer symbols than shown.

It then sets `outbid = highestBidder` with no `outbid != msg.sender` check (:231-234). The existing test `testSelfOutbidFullyFundedAndLiabilitiesConserved` (test/KilimAuction.t.sol:101-108) asserts this: 25 then 27 from one wallet gives 52 credits.
- The reward is on the full amount and is never removed. `rewardForBid` (src/KilimAuction.sol:152-154) returns `min(min(amount / tokenUnit, maxSymbolsPerBid), symbolCap - symbolsAllocated)`. `_bid` (:130-149) adds it to `symbolCredits` and `symbolsAllocated` (:142-143); nothing decrements them on outbid.
- The refund is paid inside the same call. `_refundOutbid` (ERC20EnglishAuction.sol:263-272) self-calls `payOutbidRefund` with 150,000 gas (:26, :265), which is enough for a contract with a plain `receive()`. A contract looping `bid` externally is not stopped by `nonReentrant`, because each call completes before the next.
- No per-bid cap exists at launch. The constructor allows `maxSymbolsPerBid == symbolCap` (KilimAuction.sol:93-94). The deploy script pins both to 1,000,000 on chain 1 (script/DeployKilim.s.sol:79-80, :425-428), matching deploy/mainnet.example.json:25-26.

Using `minimumBid()` exactly (ERC20EnglishAuction.sol:161-166: ceil 10%, then ceil to 0.001 ETH) from the 0.01 ETH reserve, the 93rd bid is 93.862 ETH and `symbolsAllocated` reaches 1,000,000. Cumulative bids are 1,031.969 ETH. Peak attacker balance is about 179 ETH (bid 92 of about 85.3 ETH is still escrowed while bid 93 is paid).

The ladder threshold is the same about 91-94k units in both modes: USDC bound at about $91k final, ETH binds at about 93.9 ETH final. At any ETH price above roughly $1,000 that is harder to reach in dollar terms, not easier. AUDIT.md:39 ("no binding cap ... cannot exhaust a pool") was equally inaccurate for USDC; this is a stale-documentation issue, not a regression introduced by the on-disk change.

findings.title: Risk-free symbol farming by inserting a self-outbid ladder in front of a pending jump bid
findings.description:
K-01 was accepted on the reasoning that a wallet holding the top bid pays for it if nobody outbids it. With a public mempool that risk disappears whenever a pending bid is at least two steps above the current price: an attacker can ladder up to just under it in the same block, knowing the pending bid will outbid and refund them.

The site sends expectedFirstSymbolId = 0 by default (lockIds is off) and minimumReward equal to the quote, so the victim's bid still succeeds unless the pool is nearly empty. The victim loses no ETH, but the symbol IDs (and so the public traits) they receive move, and the attacker takes roughly 11 times the gap in symbols for gas only. Because traits are public (K-02), the attacker can size the ladder to cover rare IDs and push the victim onto common ones.

The automatic refund makes the capital round-trip complete inside the bundle. If the victim does lock IDs, any rewarded bid landing first reverts theirs with SymbolRangeMoved; an attacker using an atomic bundle simply does not land in that case.
findings.exploit_scenario:
1. Current top bid is 1 ETH. Alice submits bid(3 ETH, 3000, 0) from the site.
2. A searcher bundles in front of it a contract call that self-outbids 1.1, 1.21, ... up to about 2.7 ETH (11 bids), earning roughly 20,000 symbols. The bundle requires Alice's transaction to succeed after it.
3. Alice's bid lands, outbids the searcher, and the searcher's 2.7 ETH is refunded in the same block.
4. Net: the searcher holds about 20,000 symbols for gas (about 1M gas) with zero price risk. Alice still gets 3,000 symbols, but with IDs about 20,000 further along than quoted. If the pool had fewer than about 23,000 left, her bid reverts with RewardSlippage and the searcher's bundle is dropped.
findings.recommendation:
The measures in F-04 (per-bid cap, increment-only reward or no reward on self-outbid) shrink this too. Independently:
- Have the site show the reserved IDs and send expectedFirstSymbolId for bidders who care about traits.
- Suggest a private or protected RPC for large jump bids.
- Disclose that jump bids can be front-run for symbols.
lenses: economics, timing and MEV

findings.title: Sponsored registration (registerFor): uncapped ERC-1271 staticcall and copyable signatures let an attacker burn the sponsor's gas and budget
findings.description:
Behaviours of registerFor that cost only whoever pays for sponsored registrations; no collector funds are at risk and in every case the wallet still ends up registered or the slot is gone.

- **Uncapped ERC-1271 call.** For a wallet with code (including an EIP-7702-delegated EOA), SignatureChecker makes an uncapped staticcall to wallet.isValidSignature. It is a staticcall and only 32 bytes of returndata are read, so there is no state re-entrancy and no returndata bomb. The wallet can, however, burn 63/64 of the transaction's gas and then return either answer, and can behave differently between the relayer's simulation and inclusion (keyed on block number, block.basefee or a toggled flag), consuming the relayer's full gas limit (120,000 per one reviewer's reading of the relayer).
- **Signature not bound to a submitter.** The signature is public once broadcast. Anyone who sees a pending registerFor can submit the same (wallet, deadline, signature) first; the wallet is registered as it intended, and the sponsor's transaction reverts with AlreadyRegistered (line 155) after paying gas. The wallet itself can also call register() just ahead of the sponsor.
- **Race at the cap.** Near the cap a sybil registration can take the 100th slot so the sponsor's transaction reverts with RegistrationClosed (line 150).
- **Budget drain.** One reviewer read the relayer: it serialises submissions and caps lifetime spend at 0.02 ETH with 0.00012 ETH reserved per attempt, so the loss is bounded, but about 166 scripted requests from sybil wallets exhaust the budget and real supporters then cannot use sponsorship. Another reviewer did not review the relayer. The relayer README acknowledges races and that multiple wallets can fill the slots.
findings.exploit_scenario:
Sponsor drain by hostile wallets: the attacker deploys contracts holding 0.01 ETH whose isValidSignature passes cheaply in the relayer's simulation and loops until out of gas on-chain, then posts registration requests for them. Each sponsored transaction burns its full gas limit and reverts. Repeating this empties the sponsor budget, and real supporters lose gasless registration.

Sponsor drain by sybil EOAs: the attacker scripts requests to the /register endpoint from 100 EOAs, moving the same 0.01 ETH from one to the next between requests (21,000 gas each). The sponsor pays for all 100 registrations; the attacker fills the gate for almost nothing.

Front-run: the attacker watches the mempool and resubmits each sponsored signature with a higher fee so every sponsor transaction reverts after paying base costs.
findings.recommendation:
Contract: nothing essential. If desired, cap the ERC-1271 call (for example 100k gas).

Relayer: simulate first, set a tight fixed gas limit on registerFor (an EOA registration measured about 80k; reviewers suggested about 150k as the limit), check registered[wallet] immediately before sending, treat AlreadyRegistered as success, rate-limit per requester at the proxy, consider sponsoring only EOAs without code or applying per-wallet limits, and use a private transaction route to avoid mempool copying. Keep the sponsor wallet funded only to the approved budget and treat sponsorship as best-effort.

Site: offer the direct register() path when the sponsor is out of budget, so the supporter is not left with no way to register from the page.
lenses: re-entrancy and callbacks (ETH refund call, withdraw recipients, ERC-721 receiver hooks, ERC-1271, self-calls, gas forwarding, returndata, forced reverts)
Denial of service, griefing and liveness (registration gate, refunds, extensions, settlement, prize and symbol delivery, gas caps)

SignatureChecker uses ECDSA recovery only when signer.code.length == 0. findings.title: Legacy ERC-20 mode only: a receiver that burns its per-symbol allowance but accepts makes deliverSymbols cost about 9.6M gas per 64 symbols and cannot be skipped
findings.description:
deliverSymbols skips a bidder only when deliverTo reverts (lines 194-198). A bidder contract whose onERC721Received consumes nearly the full 150k per symbol and then returns the selector succeeds, so every call spends up to 64 x 150k = 9.6M gas for 64 symbols. Line 201 then breaks without advancing the cursor while that bidder still has credits. With a large reward (maxSymbolsPerBid equals symbolCap in the launch settings) the head of the queue needs thousands of such calls, paid by whoever runs delivery, before any later bidder is reached. One self-outbid ladder also creates dozens of queue entries. Later bidders are not locked out, since claimSymbols still works, but automatic delivery is effectively stalled.

This does not affect the native-ETH launch: deliverSymbols reverts with Unauthorized there (line 179).
findings.exploit_scenario: In an ERC-20 deployment the attacker bids from a contract for 10,000 symbols early, is outbid and refunded, and keeps the credits. Its receiver hook burns about 149k gas per token and accepts. The artist's deliverSymbols(64) calls each cost about 9.8M gas and deliver only the attacker's symbols; clearing them takes 157 calls and about 1.5 billion gas before the next bidder is served.
findings.recommendation: If ERC-20 mode will never be deployed, state that the delivery queue is legacy. If it might be, move a bidder to the back or skip them after one batch, or cap symbols delivered per bidder per call so the cursor always advances.
lenses: Denial of service, griefing and liveness (registration gate, refunds, extensions, settlement, prize and symbol delivery, gas caps)
symbols, credits and the collection (KilimAuction rewards/claims/delivery, Kilim.sol mint/weave/expand/freeze/owner/royalty)

Why it is real:
- deliverSymbols advances the cursor on only two paths: the catch branch (src/KilimAuction.sol:194-198) and when the bidder's credits reach zero (:201-202). A receiver that returns the selector takes the success path (:192-193), so a bidder with credits left hits `break` at :201 and stays at the head of the queue.
- Each call's self-call gets take * 150,000 gas (:60, :189, :192), with take at most 64 (:55, :180, :185), so up to 9.6M per call. The gas guard at :190 forces the caller to supply about 9.8M or the call delivers nothing.
- Kilim.mintSymbols calls _safeMint once per token (src/Kilim.sol:240-245), so the hook runs 64 times per batch. An honest 64-symbol mint costs about 1.93M (AUDIT.md:49), about 30k per symbol, leaving roughly 115-120k per token for the hook to burn while still accepting.
- A single bidder can hold a very large credit balance: rewardForBid is min(amount / unit, maxSymbolsPerBid, remaining cap) (:153), and deploy/local.json:25-26 sets both caps to 1,000,000. Credits survive being outbid (accepted K-01; :142 is never decremented on refund).
- The claimed numbers check out: 10,000 symbols / 64 = 157 calls, times about 9.6M = about 1.5 billion gas, versus about 0.3 billion for an honest bidder of the same size. The attack is a roughly 5x gas amplification on head-of-line blocking that already exists by design.
- No existing test covers it. test/Delivery.t.sol:97-108 (testGasBurningWalletCannotStallTheQueue) uses test/mocks/GasBurner.sol, which loops until out of gas and therefore reverts and is skipped. The burn-then-accept receiver is untested.

Why it stays low:
- Native ETH mode refuses the function outright: `if (address(paymentToken) == address(0)) revert Unauthorized();` (:179).
- The mainnet deploy script refuses any nonzero payment token (script/DeployKilim.s.sol:66, :413).
- Nobody is locked out. claimSymbols (:160-166) does not depend on the queue, and symbol IDs and traits are fixed at bid time (:141), so delivery order changes nothing a collector receives.
- The only loss is gas voluntarily spent by whoever runs delivery, and they can stop at any time. The attacker pays nothing for the burn but must lock real bid capital until outbid.

One correction to the finding: the "dozens of queue entries from one self-outbid ladder" point is not an extra cost. The first entry drains all of that bidder's credits, and later empty entries are walked cheaply, up to 256 per call (:57, :183).

Docs lag: contracts/README.md:68 still says "Symbols are delivered, not claimed" and that a wallet that "burns its gas allowance" is skipped. The first is wrong for the launch mode; the second is true only if the burn causes a revert.

findings.title: The page-owner key can break royalty-paying sales or point the collection page at a hostile link
findings.description:
The owner role is correctly limited to four things: transferOwnership, renounceOwnership, setRoyaltyReceiver and setCollectionInfo. It cannot mint, burn, move tokens, change art or touch auction funds. Two of its powers still reach holders if the key (orkhanart.eth, also the treasury) is compromised or misused.

- **Royalty receiver.** setRoyaltyReceiver accepts any nonzero address, including a contract that reverts on receiving ETH or is blocked by a token issuer. Marketplaces that push the ERC-2981 amount to royaltyInfo's receiver inside the sale would then revert every such sale of every Kilim token until the owner fixes it. If the role has been renounced or lost, that state is permanent.
- **Collection link and text.** setCollectionInfo sets external_link and description to arbitrary strings. They are JSON-escaped, so the document cannot be broken, but there is no scheme or length restriction. Marketplaces show external_link as the collection's official website.

The same single address holds the treasury and this role.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker who obtains the owner key (a phished signature is enough; it is a hot-usable EOA role) calls setCollectionInfo("Claim your free weave", "https://kilim-claim.example"). Marketplace collection pages now show the attacker's site as the official link, and supporters who follow it are asked to sign approvals for their symbols.

Alternatively the attacker calls setRoyaltyReceiver(revertingContract), and listings on royalty-enforcing marketplaces fail to fill.
findings.recommendation:
The cheapest hardening is operational: hold the owner role in a multisig or hardware wallet separate from the treasury, set the final description, link and receiver once, then call renounceOwnership(). First make sure royaltyReceiver is a plain address that can always receive ETH and ERC-20s.

If a code change is acceptable before the freeze, make renouncing part of the launch checklist, or add a one-way lock for the collection info.
lenses: symbols, credits and the collection (KilimAuction rewards/claims/delivery, Kilim.sol mint/weave/expand/freeze/owner/royalty)

- `setRoyaltyReceiver` (src/Kilim.sol:180-185) rejects only `address(0)`. Any other address is accepted, including a contract that reverts on receipt, and `royaltyInfo` (:195-201) returns it unconditionally.
- `setCollectionInfo` (:188-192) stores two arbitrary strings with no scheme or length check. `contractURI` (:204-223) emits them as `description` and `external_link`.
- `_escapeJson` (:412-439) escapes `"`, `\` and control characters below 0x20, so the JSON cannot be broken or have fields injected. Existing tests at test/Kilim.t.sol:478 and :517 cover this.
- `onlyOwner` (:160-163) guards exactly four functions: `transferOwnership`, `renounceOwnership`, `setRoyaltyReceiver`, `setCollectionInfo`. None can mint, burn, move tokens, change art or touch auction funds.
- One address holds all three roles. script/DeployKilim.s.sol:68-70 sets `LAUNCH_TREASURY` and `LAUNCH_COLLECTION_OWNER` to the same `0xd664...33Ac`, the chain-1 check at :415-417 enforces it, and :401 requires `royaltyReceiver == treasury`.
- No checklist requires renouncing or a multisig. checklists/1-pre-deploy.md:21 says only that the role "can be handed over or renounced later".

**What does not hold up**
- "A phished signature is enough" is wrong for the contract as written. `onlyOwner` checks `msg.sender == owner`; there is no permit, EIP-712 or ERC-1271 path into these functions. The attacker needs a transaction sent from the owner address, meaning key theft or a phished transaction.
- That same key is the treasury. An attacker holding it can call `withdrawProceeds` and take the auction proceeds, which is far worse than anything in F-13. F-13 adds little on top of that, though it supports the suggestion to separate the roles.
- The royalty claim is conditional. Kilim.sol:194 itself notes royalties are advisory. A reverting receiver only blocks sales on marketplaces that push the ERC-2981 amount to the receiver inside the fill; nothing in the Kilim contracts reverts.
- The link attack is social engineering through a third-party marketplace page. Any loss needs a further victim action on an outside site.

**What the finding understates**
- "Until the owner fixes it" assumes the owner still has the role. An attacker with the key can set a hostile link or receiver and then call `transferOwnership(attacker)` (:166-170) or `renounceOwnership()` (:173-176). The hostile state is then permanent, because the contract is immutable and has no recovery path.

**Prior coverage**
- AUDIT.md:119 already describes the page-owner role and its limits as a design note. It is not listed among the owner-accepted findings (K-01 to K-09), so this is not a duplicate of an accepted item, but it is known behaviour.

**Severity**

findings.title: Deploy script does not pin the motif set or measure tokenURI read gas, and the site still expects 812 motifs while the decision is 1,024
findings.location: script/DeployKilim.s.sol:277-305 and :410-432; site/chain.js:12 and :178; scripts/site-config.mjs:56-57; deploy/sepolia.example.json:9-13; onchain/build/manifest.json; test/render/RenderGasLimits.t.sol; launch/DECISIONS.md
findings.description:
launch/DECISIONS.md fixes the motif library at 1,024 and says the 1,024 set must be packed, rendered and verified before deployment. Three things on disk do not enforce that:

- **No motif pin on chain 1.** _requireLaunchSettings pins every auction value but not motifCount or the content hashes. The store on disk (onchain/build/manifest.json) and the Sepolia template are still the 812 pack. A mainnet runStore/runAuction from the current build would pass every guard and fix 812 motifs forever.
- **No read-gas ceiling in the script.** _checkRenderer calls masterpieceURI(), symbolURI() and artworkURI() in simulation and compares hashes, but never measures gas. MAX_TX_GAS only covers deployment transactions. The 812 pack already reads the 1/1 at about 22.4M gas with a 24M target, and checklists/1-pre-deploy.md says only about 90 more median symbols fit. A 1,024 pack would land well above that. The only guard is test/render/RenderGasLimits.t.sol, which is a test run, not a deploy-time refusal.
- **Site pins 812.** chain.js refuses to start, and site-config.mjs refuses to write the config, if collection.motifCount() is not 812. If the auction is deployed with the decided 1,024 pack, the site fails closed until both are changed.

No funds are at risk; transfers, bids and claims never call the renderer. The risk is a permanent, unfixable display problem for the 1/1 and large artworks on RPC endpoints that cap eth_call (K-03 already notes some cap at 25M), or a launch-day site outage.
findings.exploit_scenario: No attacker needed. The operator packs the 1,024 set, runs runStore and runAuction on mainnet; every script check passes. The 1/1's tokenURI now costs more than some marketplaces' or wallets' eth_call cap, so the winner's 1/1 shows blank there, permanently. Separately, the site shows a fatal startup error ("collection.motifCount() is 1024, the site draws 812") until it is rebuilt.
findings.recommendation: In _checkRenderer, measure gasleft() around masterpieceURI() and a worst-case artworkURI() and refuse above the published ceilings. On chain 1, pin motifCount (and ideally the three hashes) as launch constants once the set is final. Change MOTIFS in site/chain.js and the 812 check in site-config.mjs in the same commit as the final pack.
lenses: deployment, configuration and integration

skeptic.reasoning:
Every factual claim checks out on disk, but two of the three parts are open launch items the checklist already tracks, not hidden defects. Only the missing deploy-time read-gas refusal is a real gap. No funds or NFTs are at risk in any branch. I did not run forge; this is a code and document trace.

- `_requireLaunchSettings` (script/DeployKilim.s.sol:410-432) pins eleven auction values plus the nonce and lead time; `motifCount` and the three content hashes are absent, and no `LAUNCH_` constant exists for them (:66-81).

- So deploying 812 against the 1,024 decision (launch/DECISIONS.md:7, :24) needs the operator to copy 812 values in by hand and skip sign-off. That is a process slip, not a code path that fails silently.

**2. No read-gas ceiling in the script: true, and the only substantive part.**
- `_checkRenderer` (:277-305) compares immutables, the chunk list and three golden sha256 values. It never measures gas.
- `MAX_TX_GAS = 8_000_000` (:57) is applied only to deployment transactions (:369-373, :521-528).

- `site/chain.js:12` sets `MOTIFS = 812`; `:178` throws a Startup error on mismatch unless `opts.motifCount` is passed.

- `checklists/1-pre-deploy.md:80` already says to "update the site's motif count (812 today)" after the final pack.
- The effect is a site that refuses to start, not a wrong display or a wrong transaction.

findings.title: Forced ETH, and refunds owed to bidder contracts that cannot receive ETH and cannot call withdrawRefund, are locked permanently
findings.description:
There is no receive/fallback, so ordinary stray sends revert. ETH forced in via selfdestruct or as a block reward is not counted anywhere and has no exit (K-06, accepted).

The automatic refund goes to the bidding address. If that address is a contract whose receive reverts or needs more than 150k gas, the amount moves to refunds[bidder], and only that same address (msg.sender) can call withdrawRefund(to). A helper, router or minimal bidder contract that bids on a user's behalf, rejects ETH and has no function to call withdrawRefund locks its user's ETH permanently, since there is no admin rescue.

findings.title: A bid has no deadline, so a pending transaction can land much later at the price the bidder signed
findings.description:
bid(amount, minimumReward, expectedFirstSymbolId) stays valid for as long as amount still meets the minimum and the auction is open. A jump bid signed with a low fee can sit in the mempool and execute hours later, when the bidder may no longer want it. Whoever orders the block also chooses where it lands relative to other bids (see F-07).

No ETH is lost beyond the bid the user signed, and they can cancel by replacing the nonce.
findings.exploit_scenario: Alice signs a 5 ETH jump bid with a low priority fee while the price is 1 ETH, sees it stuck, and assumes it failed. Two hours later the base fee drops, the transaction is included, and she becomes leader at 5 ETH. Her ETH is locked until she is outbid, or she wins.
findings.recommendation: Optional: add a deadline parameter to bid (revert if block.timestamp > deadline). Otherwise have the site surface pending bids clearly and offer a cancel (nonce replacement).
lenses: economics, timing and MEV

The only time checks in `_handleBid` are `settled`, `block.timestamp < startsAt`, and `started && block.timestamp >= endsAt` (contracts/src/auction/ERC20EnglishAuction.sol:221-224).
- **The auction can stay open indefinitely.** With no bids it never closes, and every late bid pushes `endsAt` to now + `extensionWindow` with no cap (ERC20EnglishAuction.sol:236-244). - **Exposure is bounded to the signed amount.** In ETH mode `msg.value` must equal `amount` (ERC20EnglishAuction.sol:249-251), so the bidder pays exactly what they signed; no third party can profit from this or raise the price.
- **The two existing guards stop only some stale bids.**

In the normal case the reward is unchanged and the stale bid passes.

findings.title: Chain-1 guard accepts any nonzero inspection window, and config integers are narrowed without a range check
findings.description:
Two small gaps in the mainnet guard; neither produces a broken auction on its own.

- `minLeadSeconds` only has to be nonzero on chain 1, so a value of 1 passes. The inspection window between deployment and startsAt is what lets collectors verify an immutable contract before registration opens; the checklist suggests 24 hours but the script would accept one second.
- loadConfig casts JSON integers straight to uint8, uint16 and uint64 (tokenDecimals, incrementBps, maxCells, startsAt, duration, extensionWindow). An out-of-range value wraps silently instead of being refused; for example incrementBps 66536 becomes 1000 and passes the pin. The deployed value is still the pinned one, so this is harmless on chain 1, but on Sepolia a typo could deploy a different value than the file shows.
findings.exploit_scenario: Not an attack. An operator under time pressure sets minLeadSeconds to a small value to get past a refusal; registration and bidding open minutes after deployment, before anyone has checked the published addresses, hashes and trait layout.
findings.recommendation: Pin a minimum on chain 1 (for example `minLeadSeconds >= 86400`) and refuse any config integer that does not fit its target type before casting.
lenses: deployment, configuration and integration

**1. Inspection window (confirmed)**
- `script/DeployKilim.s.sol:431` is the only chain-1 constraint on the window: `if (c.minLeadSeconds == 0) revert Refused(...)`. There is no lower bound.
- `:148` reads `minLeadSeconds` as a raw uint256, and `:358` only requires `a.startsAt >= block.timestamp + c.minLeadSeconds`. With `minLeadSeconds = 1`, a `startsAt` a few seconds after the simulation timestamp passes.

- Mitigations: `_printSettings` prints `minLeadSeconds` and "in N s" for `startsAt` (`:451-457`), so the operator sees the value. In ETH mode bidding also needs 100 registrations, and a short window does not change contract behaviour or put funds at risk. It is an operational-process gap, not an exploit.

**2. Narrowing casts (confirmed)**
- `loadConfig` casts `parseJsonUint` results (uint256) with explicit casts, which truncate silently in Solidity 0.8: `uint8` at `:146`, `uint64` at `:152-154`, `uint16` at `:155` and `:159`. `:342` also casts `uint16(c.motifCount)`.

- `motifCount` is the one narrowed value that is caught: the read-back at `:402` compares `k.motifCount()` against the uint256 `c.motifCount`.

findings.title: Minor surviving mutants: deadline boundary, Registered event count, 2,300-gas ETH payout, refund/collect order, withdrawProceeds reentrancy guard
findings.description:
These mutants survive with limited impact:
(a) `block.timestamp > deadline` changed to `>=`: no test registers exactly at the deadline.
(b) `emit Registered(wallet, registrationCount++)`: no test checks the event's count, which an indexer or the site may use for progress to 100.
(c) ETH _pay with `gas: 2300`: no ETH-mode test pays a contract recipient that needs more than the stipend (a Safe, a 4337 account, a 7702-delegated EOA) through refund, withdrawRefund or withdrawProceeds. Such recipients would silently fall to pull refunds or revert on withdrawal.
(d) _refundOutbid before _collectBid: the documented order ('MUST call _collectBid and then _refundOutbid') is not enforced by a test.
(e) nonReentrant removed from withdrawProceeds: no test re-enters from the proceeds recipient. The function follows checks-effects-interactions, so the on-disk code is safe.
findings.exploit_scenario: No direct attack on the on-disk code. Example of what could slip through: an edit adds a 2,300-gas stipend to ETH payouts 'for safety'; tests pass; after deployment every Safe-based collector's automatic refund is deferred and a Safe treasury's withdrawProceeds(to = Safe) reverts until a plain EOA recipient is used.
findings.recommendation: Add small tests: registerFor at block.timestamp == deadline succeeds; expectEmit Registered(wallet, 1) and (wallet, 100); refund, withdrawRefund and withdrawProceeds to a receiver that does an SSTORE and emits an event in receive(); a re-entering proceeds recipient cannot call withdrawProceeds, withdrawRefund or claimPrize; a rejected deposit leaves the previous leader unrefunded and still leading in ETH mode.
lenses: Test adequacy by mutation (working tree, ETH launch mode)
